# Incident Report: PCAP Traffic Analysis — 2021-09-10-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap

**Evidence base:** Single PCAP file (9,221 packets, 2021-09-11 03:15:07 to 04:31:57 UTC, ~76.8 min). No Suricata/IDS alert exports were present in the evidence directory — all findings below are derived directly from packet analysis with tshark.

## Victim host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.9.10.102** |
| MAC address | **00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-KKITB6Q** (confirmed via DHCP option 12, NBNS name registration, and AD computer object `CN=DESKTOP-KKITB6Q,CN=Computers,DC=angrypoutine,DC=com`) |
| Logged-in domain user | **hobart.gunnarsson** (Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString, realm `ANGRYPOUTINE.COM`) |
| Windows domain | ANGRYPOUTINE.COM (workgroup/NetBIOS name ANGRYPOUTINE; DC at 10.9.10.9, ANGRYPOUTINE-DC) |

## Malware family and attribution

**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alerts were provided with this evidence, so no rule-based signature match exists to cite. Based on the observed infection chain, the traffic pattern is consistent with **IcedID (aka BokBot)**:

- Delivery via a fake-update-style lure domain serving a payload at a randomized, multi-segment URI path, returned as `application/octet-stream`.
- The downloaded payload is a **PE32+ DLL (x86-64)** exporting `DllRegisterServer`/`DllUnregisterServer` — the standard IcedID loader export convention (loaded via `regsvr32.exe`/`rundll32.exe`).
- Immediately after the download, the host performs a short TLS handshake to an initial C2 IP, then transitions to long-duration, low-frequency periodic TLS beaconing (roughly every 5–6 minutes) to a second IP for the remainder of the capture — consistent with IcedID's persistent C2 check-in behavior.
- Both C2 IPs present the **identical self-signed TLS certificate** (CN `londonareloeli.uk`), indicating shared/rotated malware infrastructure rather than legitimate distinct services.
- Post-infection the host generates heavy LDAP/SAMR/DCE-RPC/Kerberos/NBNS traffic against the domain controller (10.9.10.9) — consistent with IcedID's known internal domain/network reconnaissance phase.
- The host also queried `myexternalip.com`, a public-IP self-check commonly performed by this loader family.

No family name string, YARA match, or config extraction was possible from packet data alone, so treat the "IcedID" label as an assessment, not a confirmed identification.

## Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in traffic)

**Malicious domain / delivery:**
- `simpsonsavingss.com` → resolved to `194.62.42.206`

**Malicious URL (payload delivery):**
- `http://simpsonsavingss.com/bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/MLdmpfjaX/5uFG3Dz7yt/date1?BNLv65=pAAS` — HTTP GET at t=139.7s (relative), 200 OK, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, 284,816 bytes

**Transferred file:**
- Retrieved filename in URL: `date1` (query string `BNLv65=pAAS`)
- File type: PE32+ DLL (x86-64), MZ header, exports `DllRegisterServer`/`DllUnregisterServer`
- **SHA256: `eed363fc4af7a9070d69340592dcab7c78db4f90710357de29e3b624aa957cf8`**

**Command-and-control endpoints:**
- **167.172.37.9:443** — initial post-infection TLS check-in, single session, t≈144.1s, self-signed cert CN=`londonareloeli.uk`
- **94.158.245.52:443** — persistent C2, ~34 discrete TLS sessions from t≈148.7s through t≈4512.3s (end of capture), same self-signed cert CN=`londonareloeli.uk` reused across every session, beacon interval settling to roughly every 300–360 seconds after an initial burst of 4 quick connections

**Supporting behavioral indicator:**
- DNS/HTTPS query to `myexternalip.com` (34.117.59.81) at t≈253.8s — public-IP self-check typical of this loader

## Not malicious (verified, ruled out during triage)
Traffic to Microsoft Windows Update/Delivery Optimization (`download.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`), Microsoft NCSI, Office 365, `login.live.com`, Bing/MSN, `store-images.s-microsoft.com`, `update.googleapis.com`, and internal AD/DNS/DHCP/mDNS/SSDP chatter are all legitimate and consistent with normal Windows enterprise endpoint behavior — excluded from IOCs above.
